What do Class A–E actually mean?Thresholds behind CPCB's full designated-best-use scale.
Class ADrinking water source, without conventional treatment but after disinfection. The cleanest tier. Requires DO ≥ 6 mg/L, BOD ≤ 2 mg/L.
Class BOutdoor bathing (organised). Safe for recreational contact. Requires DO ≥ 5 mg/L, BOD ≤ mg/L.
Class CDrinking water source, but only after conventional treatment and disinfection. Requires DO ≥ 4 mg/L, BOD ≤ mg/L.
Class DPropagation of wildlife and fisheries. Requires pH , DO ≥ mg/L, free ammonia ≤ mg/L.
Class EIrrigation, industrial cooling, controlled waste disposal. The lowest tier, essentially unfit for contact. Requires pH –, conductivity ≤ 2250 µS/cm, SAR ≤ 26, boron ≤ 2 mg/L, no DO or BOD floor.

Source: CPCB, Designated Best Use Water Quality Criteria. These are fixed regulatory thresholds, not a statistical pattern. The class legend under the map above shows only the classes actually present in the current data.

Dissolved oxygen: best and worst off

Dissolved oxygen (DO) is the clearest read on the lake's oxygen budget. The CPCB Class D condition is 4 mg/L or more. The highest of the latest dissolved-oxygen readings is mg/L, but that one number undersells the spread: in KSPCB's latest round alone, clear the 4 mg/L bar Select a lake name to open it on the Explore map.

Lowest dissolved oxygen: worst off
Highest dissolved oxygen: best off

Total dissolved solids: distribution across lakes

Each bar counts lakes by their latest recorded TDS concentration, not individual monthly samples. The dashed line marks the BIS 10500 acceptable drinking-water limit of mg/L, a reference rather than a lake-ecology standard. Dissolved minerals and salts contribute to TDS. Hardness primarily reflects calcium and magnesium and is not equivalent to TDS.

pH

The dashed lines mark the CPCB Class D pH reference band (). Readings within that range do not, by themselves, show that a lake is healthy: dissolved oxygen, organic pollution, nutrients and microbial contamination must be considered separately. The bars count samples rather than distinct lakes.

The cloudiest lakes

Ranks lakes by the median of their monthly turbidity readings, in nephelometric turbidity units (NTU), requiring at least measured months. Metals are tested in , not every month. Blue bars show the share of samples with a detectable reading. Red bars show the share exceeding the corresponding IS 10500 drinking-water reference limit.

Chronic hypoxia leaderboard

Bars show the share of recorded months with dissolved oxygen below mg/L. This measures how often low oxygen was observed. It does not measure the severity of individual readings. Select a lake name to open it in Explore.

COD:BOD ratio, by lake

Bars show each lake’s median monthly COD:BOD ratio. The median across eligible lakes is . A higher ratio means more COD relative to BOD. It does not establish an industrial source. Select a lake name to open it in Explore.

Fecal coliform: is the water safe?

Fecal coliform is a standard proxy for pathogen risk from waste. A lake with relatively low BOD or acceptable oxygen can still have high fecal contamination. Unlike BOD, DO and nitrogen measures, fecal coliform is a microbiological indicator, so it can move independently of the chemistry. Ranked by median monthly reading, lakes with sparse monitoring histories excluded. CPCB's organized-bathing criterion for fecal coliform is 500 MPN/100mL desirable and 2,500 maximum permissible. The 5,000 MPN/100mL Class C criterion applies to total coliform, not fecal coliform. Select a lake name to open it in Explore.

Ammoniacal N vs. nitrate: reduced and oxidized nitrogen

Ammoniacal N (NH3 + NH4+, reported as N) is reduced nitrogen. Nitrate is a more oxidized form. Nitrification can move ammonia through nitrite toward nitrate, consuming oxygen and alkalinity, but the relative amounts also depend on loading, oxygen, temperature, biology and residence time. This chart therefore compares nitrogen oxidation state. It does not date a discharge. Ranked by ammoniacal N's share of (ammoniacal N + nitrate), medians per lake, with sparse histories or negligible ammoniacal N excluded. Select a lake name to open it on the Explore map.

Seasonal comparison: wetter and drier months, citywide

The pre-monsoon squeeze

The citywide monthly medians echo the paired-station seasonal comparison: June–December generally has higher dissolved oxygen and lower BOD than January–May. Cooler water can hold more oxygen, but the temperature shift explains only part of the observed DO difference. Lower BOD in the same period is consistent with reduced oxygen demand contributing as well. These are seasonal associations, not proof of a single cause.

Dissolved oxygen (mg/L): higher is healthier BOD (mg/L): higher is worse

You do not need a lab for a first read.

You can make useful first observations without a laboratory. These are portable tools a lake-walk volunteer can carry. None replaces certified lab testing, but each is enough to flag a lake worth a closer look.

pH strips or pen
₹150–₹500. Flags acid mine drainage or industrial discharge fast. CPCB's own Class D criteria (wildlife and fisheries) sets as the acceptable range.
TDS / EC pen
₹300–₹800. One number for total dissolved salts: a fast, blunt proxy for how much has leached or been dumped into the water.
Hardness test strips
₹200 per pack. Reads Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ as CaCO₃ equivalent: mostly geology, but a useful cross-check parameter.
Secchi disk / turbidity tube
₹0–₹200 (DIY). Measures how far light penetrates: a rough proxy for algae load and suspended sediment.
Dissolved oxygen field kit
₹800–₹1,500 for a colorimetric titration kit. Low DO is one of the clearest signs of organic pollution and fish stress.
Thermometer
₹50. Sounds trivial, but temperature shifts change how much oxygen water can hold, providing context for every other reading.

Prices are indicative and may vary. Regulatory criteria cited for these tools are documented in Sources & Methods.

A city that grew over its own water.

Bengaluru's lakes were built to solve a practical problem. With no major river nearby, generations of builders stored monsoon rain in artificial tanks, or keres, across the Koramangala–Challaghatta, Hebbal and Vrishabhavathi valleys. Channels called rajakaluves connected many of them in cascades, so overflow from one tank could reach another. The network supplied water for irrigation and everyday use, while sustaining wetlands around the tanks.

As the city grew and piped supplies gradually replaced the tanks, many feeder channels were severed and lakebeds took on other uses. Parts of the former Dharmambudhi Tank became a bus stand. Parts of Sampangi Lake became stadium grounds. Other lakes survived but lost catchment land, received sewage through their drains, or became isolated from neighbouring water bodies. Conservation efforts have restored some lakes, but the network is far more fragmented than it once was. IISc Energy & Wetlands Research Group →

Sewage & grey water
Untreated or partially treated inflow is the most consistent driver of nutrient overload in the city's lake network.
Encroachment
Shrinking catchment area means less natural filtration before runoff reaches open water.
Detergent phosphate
A major contributor to the foam and algal bloom events that make national headlines each monsoon.
Broken lake chains
Severed rajakaluves and isolated lakes disrupt the cascades that once moved monsoon water across the city.

Foam on Bellandur and Varthur, fish kills after hot spells and persistent algal blooms are visible signs of pressure on the surviving lakes. Water-quality measurements help put those events in context.

Encroachment, in real published numbers.

The figures below come from different years, surveys and definitions of Bengaluru, so they cannot be treated as a single citywide estimate. The numbers are drawn from published sources rather than calculated here, and the differences between them matter. A 2007 IISc survey found that 72% of Greater Bengaluru's lakes had lost catchment area. A 2024 IISc study reported lake-level encroachment at 98%. Although the measures are not directly comparable, the findings consistently point to extensive encroachment and catchment loss, not to one definitive percentage.

Chemistry Lens.

The readings make more sense as a connected system than as isolated numbers. Organic matter and nitrification consume oxygen. Alkalinity buffers the acidity produced as ammonia is oxidized. pH controls how much total ammoniacal nitrogen is present as un-ionized NH3. Phosphorus availability can feed biological production that later returns to the oxygen budget. Four reactions sit behind those readings:

1. Oxygen budget

BOD tracks biological oxygen demand, while COD tracks a broader chemically oxidizable load. Ammonia can add a separate nitrogenous demand: complete nitrification requires about 4.57 mg O2 per mg ammonia-N. For physical scale, freshwater oxygen saturation at 25 °C is about 8.3 mg/L at sea level and about 7.4 mg/L at Bengaluru's roughly 920 m elevation.

2. Ammonia speciation

KSPCB reports total ammoniacal N, not free ammonia. At 25 °C and pH 7.4, only about 1.4% is un-ionized NH3. The fraction rises to about 15% by pH 8.5. That is why a total-ammonia reading cannot be compared directly with CPCB's free-ammonia limit.

3. Carbonate buffering

Alkalinity is the water's acid-neutralizing reserve, dominated in most of these lakes by bicarbonate. Nitrification consumes about 7.14 mg/L of alkalinity as CaCO3 per mg/L ammonia-N oxidized, linking nitrogen chemistry to pH stability.

4. Phosphorus and redox

Ortho-phosphate is the dissolved inorganic phosphorus form most directly available for uptake. Under anoxia, iron-bound phosphorus can sometimes be released from sediment through reductive dissolution, but that mechanism remains a hypothesis here: iron is reported in only 612 records (14.2%) and redox potential is not reported.

Data sources.

Where the water-quality records, scientific references and contextual evidence used by the project come from.

Water-quality data

  • KSPCB monthly reports: Monthly water-quality reports published by the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board. Data as of . kspcb.karnataka.gov.in →
  • Coordinates and lake matching: KSPCB-monitored lakes carry their source coordinates where available. Lakes without a KSPCB coordinate are matched against lake geodata published by the Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE), Bengaluru, through its Centre for Social and Environmental Innovation (CSEI), in the “Crowdmapping Bengaluru's lakes” project →, using canonicalized names and coordinate proximity. A handful of matches required editorial judgment.

Scientific references

  • Water-quality criteria and LPI benchmarks: CPCB designated-best-use criteria, BIS 10500 drinking-water limits where explicitly used as reference values, and the cited project screening anchors are documented in the Lake Pressure Index table below.
  • Chemistry: Oxygen solubility, ammonia speciation, nitrification stoichiometry and phosphorus-redox references are kept beside the explanation they support on Chemistry Lens →

Context evidence

  • Lake history and encroachment: IISc Energy & Wetlands Research Group / Bangalore Urban Information System, the 2015 Comptroller and Auditor General performance audit, and Deccan Herald reporting. The published figures and caveats are collected under Background →
  • Lake restoration and persistent urban pressures: Ramachandra, T. V., Sincy, V., & Asulabha, K. S. (2020). Efficacy of rejuvenation of lakes in Bengaluru, India. Green Chemistry & Technology Letters, 6(1), 14–26. View source →
  • Documented lake cascade and animation: The downstream connections from Kattigenahalli through Kogilu Kere, Jakkur Lake, Rachenahalli Lake, Kalkere Tank and Rampura Lake to Yelemallappa Shetty Lake are listed in Table 2 of Kulranjan & Srinivasan (2026), Frontiers in Water ↗. See ATREE-CSEI's mapped stream network ↗ for detailed channel geometry. The animation is illustrative, not a surveyed flow path or travel-time model.
  • Satellite imagery: Esri World Imagery Wayback (Esri, Maxar, Earthstar Geographics), releases dated and , chosen to match season. livingatlas.arcgis.com/wayback → A two-frame comparison cannot show what happened in between, and image resolution varies by location.

Data Pipeline

How monthly KSPCB PDFs are harmonized, matched and checked without silently replacing suspect readings.

The monthly KSPCB PDFs are turned into a harmonized dataset while preserving raw values. Fields are standardized, station identities and lake locations are reconciled, and data-quality flags are attached rather than silently replacing suspect measurements.

Checks include implausible extremes, station-name collisions, fecal-coliform values above total coliform, and disagreement between reported SAR and an ion-based recomputation. Corrections are made only when the source report or a documented extraction rule supports them. Statistical outliers remain in the reference dataset and can be reviewed separately under Data Errors →

The Lake Pressure Index

How oxygen, nutrients and fecal contamination are combined into a transparent project screening score.

Data Quality Notes

What extraction gaps, reporting ambiguities and measurement caveats mean for interpreting the dashboard.

Extraction and matching issues

  • Two river monitoring stations are included without a KSPCB location. KSPCB's own dataset carries readings for two river stations (River Arkavathi at Tippagondanahalli Reservoir, River Dakshina Pinakini near Mugalur Bridge) but never populated a latitude/longitude for either, unlike every lake in the file. Where shown on the map, their positions are an editorial addition, not a KSPCB-supplied figure: they are placed using independent hydrological references for the named site (a reservoir, a named bridge crossing) rather than a coordinate that came from KSPCB itself.
  • Lake names are not reliable identifiers. Two different lakes can share the exact same name. Puttenahalli Lake, for example, is the name of more than one lake in this dataset. When a measurement from such a lake arrives without a station code, coordinates, or ward, there is no way to distinguish between them. A single lake can also appear under different casing, punctuation, and spelling across months.
  • Coordinates and station codes are often absent, or occasionally duplicated, at the source. Many lake rows carry no station number, latitude, or longitude in the PDF itself. Where possible these are filled in by matching against an external lake-geodata catalogue, not by KSPCB. When a station code is missing, the measuring station is identified instead using the canonicalized lake name and, where needed, its latitude and longitude. Occasionally two distinct lakes carry the exact same coordinate for no apparent reason: Ramammana Kere and Arashinakunte Kere share an identical latitude/longitude in the source data despite being different lakes.
  • Whole months are missing from the archive. November 2023, for instance, has no report at all, for any lake.
  • Some PDFs do not state their own month or year. That has to be inferred from the filename or an earlier page, which is occasionally wrong for a stray or mislabeled page.
  • Format changes from file to file, and columns get silently dropped. Column layout, font, and even which fields are present at all vary month to month, so no single parsing rule works across the whole archive. The ETL step has to detect and adapt to each format on its own. Station code is one recurring casualty: some months' files omit that column entirely rather than leaving it blank.
  • Lake names sometimes come through corrupted from the source file. KSPCB's own files sometimes replace "na" with a hyphen inside a lake name: "Basavanapura Lake" becomes "Basava-pura Lake," "Anjanapura Lake" becomes "Anja-pura Lake," and so on. Separately, a lake name that wraps onto a second line in the KSPCB PDF is sometimes truncated instead of continued, so only the first line survives extraction and the name comes through garbled or cut short.
  • Text sometimes gets garbled or cut short by the PDF itself. Where a PDF's columns are too tight, characters from adjacent cells bleed into each other on extraction, occasionally scrambling a lake name. Separately, some lake names and other fields are already cut short in the source file itself, before extraction ever runs.
  • Source is PDF only, never CSV. KSPCB publishes these monthly reports as PDFs, not machine-readable tables, so every number here first went through PDF-to-text extraction rather than a clean data feed.

Measurement caveats

  • A number of readings look like errors. Fecal coliform is extremely right-skewed (median MPN/100mL across all samples) with a long tail into the tens of millions: Kammasandra Lake and Gangondanahalli Lake both spike that high more than once, and one reading, Andhrahalli Lake in Jan 2024, hits 3.3 billion. It is excluded from the Dashboard's charts rather than plotted on a scale that hides everything else. Phosphate has a similar outlier: Yediyur Tank's Feb 2024 reading of 22.0 mg/L sits roughly 50× the dataset's typical range. SAR (Sodium Adsorption Ratio) readings above 30, including Chikkagubi Lake's Apr 2026 reading of 786, showed a recurring pattern: a dropped decimal point. SAR can be recomputed independently from a sample's own sodium, calcium, and magnesium readings, using SAR = Na⁺ / √((Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺) / 2), with all three ions expressed in meq/L. Doing so for Chikkagubi's Apr 2026 row gives 7.86, not 786, a hundredfold difference consistent with a misplaced decimal point rather than a real reading. The pipeline checks every SAR value against this recomputed figure and logs any where the two disagree by more than rounding error, so readings with that mismatch are flagged. Kempambudhi Tank's Apr 2024 phosphate reading of 94.0 mg/L is almost certainly meant to read 0.94 (its source row is also missing TDS and TSS, consistent with a truncated or malformed row), and Kudlu Doddakere's Sep 2023 pH reading of 1.9 looks like a stray typo, and neither has an independent value to check itself against the way SAR does. rows on file show fecal coliform reading higher than total coliform, which isn't biologically possible since fecal coliform is a subset of total coliform. These are flagged as well. May 2024 could not be checked for SAR because calcium and magnesium concentrations were unavailable for that month.
  • Phosphate and ortho-phosphate appear to be on different bases. Ortho-phosphate consistently exceeds the "total" phosphate reading, at a stable ratio across virtually every month in the dataset, close to the known conversion factor between phosphate-as-PO₄ and phosphate-as-P. Since ortho-phosphate is chemically a subset of total phosphate, it should never read higher. The most likely explanation is that one column is reported as PO₄ and the other as P, rather than a real measurement anomaly. Which column uses which basis has not been confirmed against KSPCB's own methodology, so the Lake Pressure Index treats the "phosphate" field provisionally as P and uses 0.20 mg/L as an empirical reporting-resolution anchor, not an ecological threshold. Reported zeros remain non-detects scored as zero.
  • Raw calcium and magnesium ion readings are missing for May 2024. Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ (used, among other things, to independently recompute SAR) were not published for that month, unlike the combined hardness figure.
  • Metals were tested only a few times a year. Cadmium, copper, lead, chromium, nickel, zinc, iron, and manganese were only tested in rather than monthly. Fecal streptococci is sparser:
  • BOD incubation basis is not stated in the source tables. The KSPCB reports used here label the field simply as BOD (mg/L), without an incubation time or temperature in the published table or footer. The dashboard therefore keeps the generic label BOD rather than inventing BOD3 or BOD5. Indian IS 3025 Part 44 uses 3 days at 27 °C, while CPCB designated-use BOD criteria for Classes A-C are expressed as 5 days at 20 °C. The exact KSPCB laboratory basis remains unverified from these PDFs.

Two volunteers and a newspaper article.

Aditya Rajiv Ratnam has been volunteering on Bengaluru's lakes since he was six years old, working alongside his father at citizen-run efforts such as the Puttenahalli Neighborhood Lake Improvement Trust. Long before there was a dashboard, there were two people showing up because a lake is worth showing up for, again and again, long after the headlines move on.

The spark for this project was a Deccan Herald report. It pointed out that KSPCB tests roughly 130 of Bengaluru's lakes every month, on around 30 parameters, and publishes the results, yet almost nobody outside the board has an easy way to compare those records across lakes or through time. The readings sit in PDF tables, one month at a time.

This site turns those tables into one place to explore. Readings are matched to lakes, placed on a map and followed through time, alongside satellite imagery. Most of the site is generated directly from the monthly KSPCB records. Charts, maps, rankings, class counts, seasonal comparisons and the Lake Pressure Index are all computed by script each time the site is rebuilt with a new report, and lake names are matched by documented rules instead of by hand. Written commentary is kept to the explanatory pages, such as Background, Chemistry Lens, Sources & Methods and this one. Where a record is missing, inconsistent or suspect, it is flagged openly in the Data Quality Notes, so that one can see how much weight each number can bear.

Official CPCB classes group lakes into broad bands, and nearly every lake falls in Class D or E, so they say little about how one lake differs from another. The Lake Pressure Index adds that missing resolution, making it possible to compare lakes, follow one lake through the seasons and see which kind of pressure weighs on it most. It scores every lake in every month on one scale, where 100 means the readings sit right at their benchmarks. Six measurements feed it: dissolved oxygen, BOD, ammoniacal nitrogen, nitrate, phosphorus and fecal coliform. They are grouped into oxygen and organic load, nutrients, and microbial contamination, and the three groups count equally. The resulting score is placed in one of five bands, from Good to Severe. The current cut-offs are shown in Sources & Methods. It is built from published benchmarks and clearly labelled project anchors, so anyone can recompute it from the same readings and follow exactly how a lake earned its score.

The aim is to make publicly collected lake data useful to students, researchers and neighbours who care about Bengaluru's lakes.

Research paper: Urban Lake Water Quality in Bengaluru: A Data-Driven Typology.
